name: Poland

legislature.name: Sejm (460)
legislature.detail: Not enough to override presidential vetoes (3/5 needed).

judiciary: Constitutional Tribunal and Supreme Court; legitimacy of PiS-era judicial appointments remains disputed.
synopsis: Tusk's pro-EU coalition faces a hostile, veto-wielding president, slowing judicial and social reforms. Defence spending is the highest in NATO relative to GDP.
policies: Defence spending near 5% of GDP
Restoring rule of law in the judiciary
Tighter migration and asylum suspension at Belarus border
challenges: PiS and Confederation strength ahead of 2027

name: Czechia
synopsis: Populist Babiš returned to power with nationalist and anti-Green partners; he has had to resolve conflicts of interest over his Agrofert business.
policies: Scaling back Green Deal measures
Reduced military aid to Ukraine (ammunition initiative reviewed)
Pension and energy price relief

name: Slovakia
judiciary: Constitutional Court; criminal-code and prosecutor reforms criticised by the EU.
synopsis: Fico's nationalist-left government has softened anti-corruption institutions and pursued a Russia-friendly line within the EU, sparking mass protests.
policies: Opposition to military aid for Ukraine
Fiscal consolidation package
Constitutional amendment on 'two sexes' and national sovereignty

name: Hungary

legislature.name: National Assembly (199)
legislature.detail: Fidesz under Viktor Orbán is the main opposition.

judiciary: Constitutional Court and Kúria, largely appointed under Orbán; reform is a Tisza priority.

elections.name: Parliamentary election
elections.note: Tisza ended 16 years of Fidesz rule with a two-thirds majority.

synopsis: Péter Magyar's Tisza ousted Viktor Orbán in April 2026 and is dismantling key parts of the Fidesz system while returning Hungary to the European mainstream. A constitutional amendment ended President Tamás Sulyok's mandate in July 2026, and parliament elected former Supreme Court president András Baka in his place on 11 August, with Fidesz boycotting the vote.
policies: Unlocking frozen EU funds via rule-of-law reforms
Overhaul of state media and anti-corruption measures
Lifting Hungary's vetoes on EU support for Ukraine
Cutting MPs' salaries and state waste

name: Slovenia

elections.name: Parliamentary election
elections.note: Golob's Freedom Movement won most votes but could not form a majority.

synopsis: Janez Janša returned as PM for a fourth time in mid-2026, leading a right-leaning coalition after Robert Golob failed to build a majority.
policies: Tax cuts
Targeted spending
Anti-corruption drive

name: Romania

legislature.name: Chamber of Deputies (331)
legislature.detail: Bolojan lost a no-confidence vote on 5 May 2026 (PSD + AUR). Parliament approved Niculescu's cabinet on 20 October 2026 by 280 votes (233 needed), with PSD, PNL and UDMR in favour; PNL and UDMR hold no ministries and call themselves opposition. AUR and USR voted against; AUR is the largest opposition force.

judiciary: Constitutional Court (annulled the 2024 presidential election) and High Court of Cassation.
synopsis: The pro-European coalition collapsed in 2026 over austerity, and Bolojan's government fell to a no-confidence vote in May. After three earlier nominees failed, non-party diplomat Luca Niculescu, President Dan's fourth nominee, won parliament's approval on 20 October 2026 for a minority cabinet of PSD ministers and independents. President Dan has ruled out early elections.
policies: Deficit reduction to below 3% of GDP by 2030, through spending efficiency and better tax collection
Flat income tax kept; minimum turnover tax (IMCA) abolished from 2027
Pension indexation from 2027 and targeted support for low-income households
Audit of central institutions to remove overlapping functions, instead of uniform staff cuts
New energy generation and storage; completion of the Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR)
Defence modernisation within NATO; support for Moldova's EU accession

name: Bulgaria
judiciary: Constitutional Court and Supreme Judicial Council; judicial reform long demanded by the EU.

elections.name: Snap parliamentary election
elections.note: Radev, who resigned the presidency to run, won outright.

elections.name: Presidential election (1st round)
elections.note: Incumbent Iliana Iotova 34.8%, former caretaker PM Andrey Gyurov 32.0% and Kostadin Kostadinov (Revival) 12.6%, on a 23% turnout; no candidate won a majority.

elections.name: Presidential runoff
elections.note: Iotova, with running mate Kiril Valchev, beat Gyurov 57.6% to 39.5% on a 28.6% turnout; Gyurov conceded. Her elected five-year term begins in January 2027.

synopsis: Former president Rumen Radev became PM in May 2026 with a rare absolute majority, ending years of repeated elections. Iliana Iotova, his vice-president and president since he resigned, won the November 2026 presidential runoff, the first woman elected to the office. Bulgaria joined the euro on 1 January 2026.
policies: Anti-corruption and judicial overhaul
Euro-area integration
Cautious stance on military aid to Ukraine
challenges: Very low turnout and voter disillusionment
reviewNote: Runoff results are near-final (Central Election Commission, 99.95% counted, 2 Nov 2026); confirm the official result.

name: Moldova
judiciary: Constitutional Court; ongoing vetting of judges.

elections.name: Parliamentary election
elections.note: PAS kept its majority despite large-scale Russian interference.

synopsis: Pro-EU PAS retained power in 2025, and Moldova is pressing ahead with EU accession negotiations. After Alexandru Munteanu resigned in July 2026, financier Vasile Tofan, nominated by President Sandu, won a confidence vote on 21 July with the votes of 53 PAS deputies.
policies: EU accession reforms
Energy independence from Russia
Judicial vetting

name: Ukraine
judiciary: Constitutional Court and Supreme Court; anti-corruption bodies NABU/SAP.

elections.name: Presidential & parliamentary elections
elections.note: Postponed while martial law is in force; to be held after hostilities end.

synopsis: Ukraine continues to resist Russia's full-scale invasion while negotiating over a possible ceasefire framework. In July 2026 parliament accepted Yulia Svyrydenko's resignation and appointed former Naftogaz head Sergii Koretskyi Prime Minister. Elections are suspended under martial law.
policies: Defence and drone production
Securing Western financing and security guarantees
EU accession reforms
Anti-corruption (after 2025 NABU controversy)
challenges: War and attacks on energy infrastructure

name: Belarus

elections.name: Presidential election
elections.note: Lukashenko's seventh term; not recognised as free by the EU.

synopsis: Lukashenko is closely aligned with Moscow and hosts Russian tactical nuclear weapons, while releasing some political prisoners in deals with the US.
policies: Union State integration with Russia
Limited prisoner releases for sanctions relief
Repression of opposition
